draft.title: The Great Depression in Australia
card: In 1929 the Wall Street crash in the United States set off a worldwide economic collapse. Countries traded less and banks became cautious.
Australia sold wool and wheat overseas, so it depended on export prices. When those prices fell, farmers and exporters earned much less.
Australia had also borrowed heavily from overseas, mainly Britain. When new loans dried up, governments struggled to pay for projects and debts.
Businesses cut staff and closed. By 1932 nearly a third of workers had no job, and many families lost their homes or relied on charity and relief work.
draft.remember: Falling export prices and lost loans pushed Australia into mass unemployment.

a.q: Why did the Wall Street crash hurt Australia so badly?
opts: Australia relied on exports and overseas loans
Australia had invested mostly in American banks
Australia's factories lost their American workers
Australia's government stopped collecting taxes
a.why: Australia earned its income from selling wool and wheat, and it borrowed from overseas. Both sources shrank after the crash. Australia did not lose its income because its own banks were in America.
a.clue: Think about what Australia sold and where it borrowed.

b.q: In 1931 Ben's wheat farm near Dubbo earns half as much as in 1928, though he grew the same amount. What best explains this?
opts: The price paid for wheat overseas fell
Ben's farm was hit by a shortage of workers
The government banned wheat from being exported
Overseas buyers wanted much more wheat
b.why: Ben grew the same amount, so the fall in his income came from a lower price. Export prices dropped sharply after the crash. A lack of workers would have cut his harvest, which did not change.
b.clue: His harvest stayed the same, so what else changed?

a.best: Australia relied on exports and overseas loans

b.best: The price paid for wheat overseas fell

problems.detail: The why's last sentence, "Australia did not lose its income because its own banks were in America", is garbled. The distractor says Australia had invested in American banks, not that its banks were in America. It could confuse a student checking their answer.

check.summary: The facts check out: the 1929 crash, falling wool and wheat prices, heavy borrowing from Britain and nearly a third of workers jobless by 1932. Both questions have one clear answer. The only problem is a confusingly worded sentence in the why for question a.
